facts.text: Coverage runs from the year to 2025-11-30 through the quarter to 2026-08-31. At 2026-08-31 the filings print debt of USD 23,912 million, cash of USD 1,220 million and liquidity of USD 5.7 billion. facts.label: Liquidity and funding float
facts.text: Liquidity at 2026-08-31 was cash of USD 1,220 million plus a revolving facility with USD 4.5 billion available, about USD 5,720 million, with USD 10.7 billion of undrawn export credit facilities that fund ship deliveries only. limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- Medium: Fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA and a printed fourth quarter 2025 are not supplied, so leverage and cover on the issuer's adjusted measure and a twelve-month adjusted EBITDA cannot be built; obtain the earnings release for the fourth quarter and fiscal 2025. - Medium: Cash interest paid is stated for fiscal years only and to the nearest USD 100 million, which limits interest cover to fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025 on a rounded basis and leaves interim cover not established; obtain interim cash interest paid. - Medium: Legal ranking within the unsecured debt is not stated in the filings and the indentures are not supplied, so the debt stack and cumulative leverage are not drawn; obtain the debt agreements. - Low: The statements print dashes for nil lines, for example debt extinguishment costs in the first half of 2026 and dividends in 2025; these cells are recorded as not supplied and not read as zero, which restricts only sums that include them. - Low: Filed totals differ from their printed parts by USD 1 million or USD 2 million: total liabilities at 2024-11-30, 2025-11-30 and 2026-08-31, the net change in cash for the first half of 2025, the first quarter of 2026 and nine months 2026, and closing cash for fiscal 2024, the first quarter of 2025, nine months 2025 and the first half of 2026; the affected cells are not supplied and no figure is plugged, while revenue lines are left as printed. - Low: No unadjusted EBITDA is stated, so statement-based EBITDA is calculated and differs from the issuer-adjusted figure by USD 19 million in Q3 2026; both are shown and the difference is not reconciled further. - Low: Total debt at 2024-11-30 is USD 27,474 million from the balance sheet lines against USD 27,475 million in the debt note, a rounding difference of USD 1 million; the balance sheet figure is used. - Low: Euro-denominated instruments are printed only as US dollar equivalents, so their euro principal is not established and no exchange rate is applied. - Low: Revolving facility availability at 2024-11-30 is not stated, so liquidity and the liquidity ratio at the end of fiscal 2024 are not calculable. - Low: Undrawn export credit facilities rose from USD 7.8 billion at 2025-11-30 to USD 10.9 billion at 2026-02-28 with no description of the new facilities; they are excluded from liquidity. - Low: The nine-month adjusted EBITDA reconciliation is not bridged because its printed parts differ from the printed total by USD 1 million; only the Q3 2026 reconciliation is bridged. - Low: The total of customer deposits at 2024-11-30 is not stated, so the trend in that funding float is shown from 2025-11-30 only.

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a benign view is that capital returns are rising while the company's own net debt to adjusted EBITDA was 3.1x at the second quarter of 2026 against its target of 2.75x, new-ship commitments of USD 18.3 billion remain, and security and guarantees have been released without the governing documents being available. A debt-funded distribution, a reversal of the release of security, a rating downgrade, or a booking slowdown that shrinks customer deposits would move the view toward higher governance and financial-policy risk; continued repayment alongside returns, with leverage reaching the target, would move it toward lower risk. facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: The balance sheet was reshaped by a refinancing program that the 2025 annual report says was completed in December 2025: in 2025 the company issued six senior unsecured note series and borrowed under three unsecured term loans, and used the proceeds with cash on hand to prepay debt of USD 11.6 billion. In December 2025 it settled the 2027 convertible notes with 69.1 million shares and USD 500 million in cash, and in the third quarter of 2026 it redeemed USD 500 million of 7.00% notes due 2029 with cash on hand. No new debt was issued in nine months 2026; the cash flow statement prints a dash for issuance proceeds. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: - Demand and pricing power are the core support, and they held through a Middle East conflict and a fuel price spike. Nine-month revenue rose 4.79% on capacity up 1.38% and unchanged occupancy of 106.5%, so growth came from price, mix and currency rather than volume, with net yields in constant currency up 2.4% in Q3 and customer deposits and 2027 bookings at record levels. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: - Margins, not revenue, are the weak point. Operating income fell USD 70 million (1.87%) in nine months on higher revenue, and the statement-based EBITDA margin eased from 28.64% to 27.51%, while fuel cost USD 223 million more and now takes 12.56% of operating costs. The company manages fuel by reducing consumption and describes no fuel hedge, so a further price rise reaches EBITDA unless yields rise with it; in the fourth quarter alone a 10% fuel move is worth USD 59 million of adjusted net income. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: - Cash generation is strong but increasingly distributed. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: - Leverage has improved because net debt fell, not because earnings grew, and the company's own 2.75x target is still USD 2,587 million of net debt away. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against caution is that demand, pricing and guidance have held through a real stress in 2026: full-year net yield guidance was cut from 2.75% in March to 1.75% in June by 1.00 percentage points and then raised to 2.3% in September, recovering 0.55 percentage points, while fuel rose 36.08% per metric ton in Q3 and the booked position for 2027 is at record levels. Accrual interest cover on statement-based EBITDA rose from 3.49x in fiscal 2024 to 5.39x in fiscal 2025 and 6.79x in nine months 2026, and the guided interest cost for fiscal 2026 is USD 218 million (16.80%) lower than in fiscal 2025. Distributions are also discretionary: the dividend is decided by the board each quarter, the repurchase program has no expiry and USD 1,562 million of it remains, so management holds a lever that does not touch debt repayment. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The view would move toward lower risk if net leverage reached 2.75x with distributions at the stated level, which needs about USD 2,587 million less net debt or higher EBITDA, if the debt agreements show wide covenant headroom, or if rating reports confirm investment grade with stable or positive outlooks. It would move toward higher risk if net yields growth fell below the guided 1.7% for Q4, if customer deposits at a quarter-end fell below the prior year, if fuel stayed above the guided USD 896 per metric ton, if distributions were funded with new debt, or if EBITDA fell by 8.71% or more at constant net debt, which would return net leverage to 3.40x. A fall of 27.48% would return it to the 4.28x of fiscal 2024. facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: The strengths, in order of weight, are pricing power with booking visibility, scale, cash generation and deleveraging, liquidity and funding access, and a mostly fixed-rate debt structure. Net yields rose through the conflict and fuel spike of 2026 and the 2027 book is at record levels; the company holds 35.65% of global cruise capacity and added 0.92% of capacity in 2025 against 4.27% for the industry, so its own supply is not what pressures price; net leverage fell from 4.28x at fiscal 2024 to 3.10x at 2026-08-31 with free cash flow of USD 3,176 million over the last twelve months; liquidity is USD 5,720 million with USD 10.7 billion of undrawn export credit facilities for ships; and 85% of debt is fixed rate, so a 100 basis point move in variable rates is worth only USD 4 million of adjusted net income in the fourth quarter. facts.label: Business and ownership
facts.text: Carnival is the largest global cruise company, with 94 ships in eight brands split between North America (64% of capacity) and Europe (36%), and a 35.65% share of global cruise capacity at the end of 2025. Tickets are 65.4% of fiscal 2025 revenue and onboard and other spending 34.6%, and guests from the United States are 55.8% of revenue, so the credit rests on North American and European leisure spending. Guests pay a deposit at booking and the balance before sailing, which gives a funding float of customer deposits of USD 7,639 million against cash of USD 1,220 million (6.26x) and a working capital deficit of USD 9.1 billion that is repaid in sailings rather than cash unless sailings are cancelled. For creditors the effect is cash flow that is visible months ahead and spread across brands, but concentrated in one product, and a float that supports liquidity in a normal booking cycle and becomes a claim in a shock. facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue is price-led, booked months ahead and discretionary. In nine months 2026 revenue rose 4.79%, onboard and other revenue rose 7.41% against 3.43% for tickets, and net yields rose 4.25% in current dollars and 2.46% in constant currency, so currency added about 1.80 percentage points, on capacity up 1.38% and occupancy unchanged; customer deposits reached records. The test of pricing power was the second quarter, when extreme geopolitical volatility hurt Mediterranean bookings and fuel was nearly 30% dearer; management chose to protect price rather than occupancy in the Mediterranean, cut full-year net yield guidance to 1.75% from 2.75%, and by September had raised it to 2.3%. The mechanism is advance booking: the book is at record levels for 2027, so a demand wobble hits a partly sold year, which supports revenue predictability for twelve months, while beyond that it remains cyclical, discretionary and weighted to the United States consumer. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Costs are largely fixed once capacity is set, so margin depends on yield outrunning cost. In nine months 2026 cruise and tour operating expenses rose 6.27% and selling and administrative expense 7.33% against revenue growth of 4.79%, so operating income fell USD 70 million and the operating margin eased from 18.47% to 17.30%. The company attributes the rise in operating expenses to fuel prices (USD 212 million), capacity (USD 170 million), currency (USD 160 million), the absence of ship-sale gains in 2025 (USD 103 million) and emission allowance costs (USD 54 million), partly offset by lower fuel use per berth day (USD 66 million). Fuel is unhedged, takes 12.56% of operating costs against 11.50% a year earlier, and cost per berth day excluding fuel rose 1.8% in Q3 in constant currency against net yields of 2.4%. Margins can be defended against volume pressure by the cost programme and by slowing capacity, but not against a sustained fuel spike without yield gains, so the cost side is average rather than strong. facts.label: Capital intensity and cash conversion
facts.text: Capital intensity is high, but new ships are largely funded by export credit. Capital expenditure was USD 3,611 million in fiscal 2025 after USD 4,626 million in fiscal 2024, and free cash flow converted 35.84% of statement-based EBITDA in fiscal 2025 and 43.44% over the last twelve months. New-ship commitments total USD 18.3 billion, of which USD 6.6 billion falls in 2027 to 2030 against export credit draws of USD 5.8 billion in those years, so 87.88% is scheduled to be externally funded and the net cash call on the company is about USD 0.8 billion, with timing differences; the cost is gross debt that rises with each delivery and is repaid over many years. Capex flexibility is limited for newbuild payments, which are contracted, and real for the non-newbuild part, which was USD 0.9 billion in Q4, so EBITDA converts into free cash flow available for debt service, although a growing share is now committed to shareholders. facts.label: Competitive forces
facts.text: Rivalry is moderate and supply-led: Carnival and its three main competitors hold about 80% of industry capacity, and in 2025 the industry added 4.27% of capacity against 0.92% for Carnival, so competitors' new ships rather than Carnival's own are the main supply threat to price. Entry is a low threat because few shipyards can build and refit large ships and the capital needed is large, with USD 18.3 billion of Carnival's own ship commitments alone. Substitutes are land-based vacations, which cap price in a downturn when households trade down. Buyers are individuals and travel agents, and commissions, transportation and other costs are 12.41% of revenue, so distribution is a real cost but no buyer has pricing leverage over the group. Suppliers matter most for shipyards, whose limited capacity can delay deliveries and refits, and for fuel, where the company is a price taker; the effect on credit is margin and delivery timing risk, not a threat to liquidity. facts.text: Strengths: pricing power with a record book, scale, deleveraging to 3.10x, USD 5,720 million of liquidity, and mostly fixed-rate debt. Liquidity is strong at USD 5,720 million with USD 10.7 billion of ship funding. Financial policy and governance are average, because returns are rising before the target and legal limits are not supplied. The trend is improving, and the missing datapoints are the debt agreements, rating levels and a fourth-quarter result. facts.label: Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds
facts.text: Over the next 12 to 24 months the company guides fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA of about USD 7.14 billion, with about USD 1.30 billion in Q4, Q4 net yields up about 1.7% in constant currency on capacity down 0.1%, and a Q4 fuel price of USD 896 per metric ton, 8.47% above Q3. Tailwinds are the record 2027 book, flat capacity growth over the next twelve months, an interest cost about USD 218 million lower in fiscal 2026 as high-coupon debt is repaid, and the first newbuild delivery in April 2027. Headwinds are fuel, the conflict, rising distributions and capex. Over three to five years the company targets return on invested capital above 16%, adjusted earnings per share growth above 50% from 2025, and about USD 14 billion of shareholder distributions to 2029 at more than 40% of cash from operations alongside 2.75x leverage; these targets support earnings growth but compete with debt reduction for cash, and are management language that the documents do not test. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The realistic downside is a summer-quarter shock that combines regional conflict or hurricane disruption with a fuel price near the guided USD 896 per metric ton. The first break is close-in bookings: in the second quarter of 2026 the company chose price over occupancy in Mediterranean sailings, and a longer episode would cost either price or occupancy in the quarter that earns about 41.92% of annual adjusted EBITDA. Because costs are largely fixed, the company's own sensitivities show how it transmits: in the June outlook a 1% change in net yields was USD 60 million of adjusted net income in the third quarter and in the September outlook USD 49 million in the fourth, and a 10% fuel move USD 59 million. At constant net debt an EBITDA fall of 8.71% returns net leverage to 3.40x and a fall of 27.48% to 4.28x. Liquidity of USD 5,720 million covers principal due to the end of 2027 2.03x, 85% of debt is fixed rate so interest cost would not spike, and the levers are to stop repurchases (USD 929 million in nine months 2026), defer non-newbuild capex and reduce the dividend. The main exposures are refunds on cancelled sailings from the USD 7,639 million deposit float, the minimum liquidity covenant of USD 1.5 billion, and refinancing the USD 3,961 million due in 2028. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress in a shock of the 2026 type, which yields rose through, but a deeper or longer shock is not tested by the documents, and the first observable signs would be deposits below the prior year and net yields below guidance. Basis: EX-99.1_2026-06-23_a20262qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 2; EX-99.1_2026-06-23_a20262qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 5; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 4; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 27; calculation U8; calculation U12; calculation X6; calculation X9; calculation X16; calculation X18; calculation X20; calculation X31; calculation X34

facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Carnival presents a strong business profile supported by pricing power, scale, a record booking position and USD 5,720 million of liquidity, but credit quality is constrained by unhedged fuel cost, rising shareholder returns before leverage reaches the 2.75x target, a USD 12,994 million maturity wall in 2027 to 2030 and legal terms that were not supplied. Cash flow durability appears adequate: free cash flow of USD 3,176 million over the last twelve months is substantial, but EBITDA is only 0.52% above fiscal 2025 and a growing share of cash is committed to shareholders. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on holding investment grade ratings and on the company keeping leverage trending toward target. The primary downside path is a summer-quarter demand or fuel shock while distributions are rising. Further analysis would require the debt agreements, the rating levels and a fourth-quarter result. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: fuel and demand shock in the summer quarter with rising distributions. ### Bottom line

The seven supplied filings and releases support the financial, business and fundamental-credit work this run requests, with limitations, so balance-sheet conclusions can rest on filed figures; covenant, security-selection and ratings conclusions cannot, because no debt agreements, indentures or rating reports were supplied.

## Request

Financial foundation for Carnival Corp Ltd. (issuer ccl) as of 2026-11-05 on the Full credit assessment pathway. It covers fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 and each quarter to 2026-08-31, in US dollars and millions. No credit recommendation is made.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Carnival's statement-based leverage fell from 4.48x total debt at the end of fiscal 2024 to 3.27x at 2026-08-31 because debt was repaid while EBITDA grew, which strengthens creditors' position; interest cover and issuer-adjusted ratios cannot be extended past fiscal 2025.
Basis: 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, pages 63–64; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; calculation V1; calculation V9

Debt at carrying value fell from USD 26,640 million at 2025-11-30 to USD 23,912 million at 2026-08-31 and cash from USD 1,928 million to USD 1,220 million, leaving net debt of USD 22,692 million, or 3.10x of last-twelve-months EBITDA of USD 7,311 million. Cash from operations of USD 5,303 million in nine months covered capital expenditure of USD 2,139 million, dividends of USD 618 million and repurchases of USD 929 million, so part of the gain is being distributed. Net debt after repurchases since 2026-08-31 is not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 9–10; calculation N5; calculation L3; calculation V10
### Leverage trajectory and drivers

Total debt over statement-based EBITDA improved from 4.48x at fiscal 2024 to 3.66x at fiscal 2025 and 3.27x at 2026-08-31, and net debt over EBITDA from 4.28x to 3.40x and 3.10x. The drivers are repayment of debt, which cut carrying value by USD 2,728 million in nine months, and EBITDA growth from USD 6,131 million to USD 7,311 million over the last twelve months. Net debt over EBITDA was 3.09x at 2026-05-31 and 3.10x at 2026-08-31, so the latest quarter added no further improvement because cash fell by USD 1,023 million. The issuer's own adjusted ratio of 3.1x at Q2 2026 uses a different EBITDA and agrees only within rounding.

Basis: 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, pages 63–64; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; EX-99.1_2026-06-23_a20262qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 3; calculation V1; calculation V2; calculation V3; calculation V4; calculation V7; calculation V8; calculation V9; calculation V10
### Coverage

Interest cover on statement-based EBITDA over cash interest paid rose from 3.83x in fiscal 2024 to 6.06x in fiscal 2025, helped by interest expense falling from USD 1,755 million to USD 1,349 million. Cash interest is printed to the nearest USD 100 million and no interim figure is stated, so cover after fiscal 2025 is not established; interest expense net of capitalized interest was USD 862 million over nine months 2026 against USD 1,034 million a year earlier.
Basis: 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, pages 63–64; 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 98; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C4; calculation C5
### Cash flow quality

Free cash flow, cash from operations less capital expenditure, was USD 2,607 million in fiscal 2025 and USD 3,164 million in nine months 2026, which is 0.36 of EBITDA in fiscal 2025. Customer deposits added USD 318 million to operating cash in nine months 2026, so part of operating cash flow is advance sales collected ahead of sailings and reverses if bookings slow. Capital expenditure fell from USD 4,626 million in fiscal 2024 to USD 3,611 million in fiscal 2025 as ship deliveries slowed.

Basis: 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 60; 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 61; 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 64; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; calculation F1; calculation F3; calculation M4
### Liquidity and funding float

Liquidity at 2026-08-31 was cash of USD 1,220 million plus a revolving facility with USD 4.5 billion available, about USD 5,720 million, with USD 10.7 billion of undrawn export credit facilities that fund ship deliveries only. Customer deposits of USD 7,639 million are an interest-free funding float that exceeds cash several times over; it is repaid in sailings rather than cash, which supports liquidity in a normal booking cycle and becomes an obligation if sailings are cancelled. Principal falling due is USD 301 million in the rest of 2026 and USD 2,517 million in 2027.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 25; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 9; calculation F2; calculation P2
### Subsequent events and conflicting figures

Repurchases after 2026-08-31 are reported only as a year-to-date total of about USD 1.2 billion at the release date, against USD 938 million used under the program by 2026-08-31, so their effect on net debt is not blended into any period figure. Nine-month repurchases are USD 929 million in the cash flow statement and USD 939 million in the equity statement, and the cash flow figure is used. Statement-based EBITDA differs from the issuer-adjusted figure by USD 19 million in Q3 2026, and both are shown.

Basis: EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 1; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 28; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 10; calculation F3
### Data quality and definitions

Several filed totals differ from their printed parts by USD 1 million or USD 2 million, including total liabilities at three balance-sheet dates and the cash roll-forward in several columns; those cells are marked not supplied rather than adjusted. Debt groups at 2025-11-30 are secured in the annual report and unsecured in the later reports, and the issuer's net debt to adjusted EBITDA definition changed between the first and second releases. The debt stack is not drawn because legal ranking is not stated.

Basis: 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, pages 63–64; 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 79; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 9; EX-99.1_2026-03-27_a20261qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 13; EX-99.1_2026-06-23_a20262qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 13

## Gaps

- Medium: Fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA and a printed fourth quarter 2025 are not supplied, so leverage and cover on the issuer's adjusted measure and a twelve-month adjusted EBITDA cannot be built; obtain the earnings release for the fourth quarter and fiscal 2025.

- Medium: Cash interest paid is stated for fiscal years only and to the nearest USD 100 million, which limits interest cover to fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025 on a rounded basis and leaves interim cover not established; obtain interim cash interest paid.

- Medium: Legal ranking within the unsecured debt is not stated in the filings and the indentures are not supplied, so the debt stack and cumulative leverage are not drawn; obtain the debt agreements.

- Low: The statements print dashes for nil lines, for example debt extinguishment costs in the first half of 2026 and dividends in 2025; these cells are recorded as not supplied and not read as zero, which restricts only sums that include them.

- Low: Filed totals differ from their printed parts by USD 1 million or USD 2 million: total liabilities at 2024-11-30, 2025-11-30 and 2026-08-31, the net change in cash for the first half of 2025, the first quarter of 2026 and nine months 2026, and closing cash for fiscal 2024, the first quarter of 2025, nine months 2025 and the first half of 2026; the affected cells are not supplied and no figure is plugged, while revenue lines are left as printed.

- Low: No unadjusted EBITDA is stated, so statement-based EBITDA is calculated and differs from the issuer-adjusted figure by USD 19 million in Q3 2026; both are shown and the difference is not reconciled further.

- Low: Total debt at 2024-11-30 is USD 27,474 million from the balance sheet lines against USD 27,475 million in the debt note, a rounding difference of USD 1 million; the balance sheet figure is used.
- Low: Euro-denominated instruments are printed only as US dollar equivalents, so their euro principal is not established and no exchange rate is applied.
- Low: Revolving facility availability at 2024-11-30 is not stated, so liquidity and the liquidity ratio at the end of fiscal 2024 are not calculable.
- Low: Undrawn export credit facilities rose from USD 7.8 billion at 2025-11-30 to USD 10.9 billion at 2026-02-28 with no description of the new facilities; they are excluded from liquidity.
- Low: The nine-month adjusted EBITDA reconciliation is not bridged because its printed parts differ from the printed total by USD 1 million; only the Q3 2026 reconciliation is bridged.
- Low: The total of customer deposits at 2024-11-30 is not stated, so the trend in that funding float is shown from 2025-11-30 only.

## Request

Business and governance for Carnival Corp Ltd. (issuer ccl) as of 2026-11-05 on the Full credit assessment pathway. It sets out the business, structure, transactions, ownership, governance, financial policy and capital allocation from the seven supplied documents. No instrument recommendation is made.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Carnival is a scaled, diversified cruise operator with no sponsor identified and now one Bermuda company, so creditor risk rests on demand, fuel and shareholder returns; legal capacity to distribute value is not established because debt agreements were not supplied.
Basis: 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, pages 7–10; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 1–5; Source readiness (CP-0)

Shareholder returns are now material: dividends of USD 618 million and repurchases of USD 929 million over nine months 2026 took 29.2% of cash from operations of USD 5,303 million, and the company targets distributing more than 40% of operating cash flow to 2029. Debt is falling and no secured debt remains, which supports creditors, but the shift from deleveraging to returns is the main governance change to monitor.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 28; EX-99.1_2026-03-27_a20261qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 3; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 3; calculation B1
### Key findings

- Scale and diversification are the core strengths: 94 ships and eight cruise lines, with North America 66.1% and Europe 31.8% of fiscal 2025 revenue and guests from the United States 55.8% of revenue, so demand and currency exposure is concentrated in US and European leisure spending.
Basis: 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 92; 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 94; calculation A1; calculation A2

- The corporate structure was simplified in May 2026: the dual listed arrangement of Carnival Corporation and Carnival plc ended in favour of one Bermuda company, Carnival Corporation Ltd., with plc shareholders exchanging one for one. The dual listed arrangement had each company cross-guarantee the other's debt; whether those cross-guarantees remain after the termination agreement is not established, because the filings say only that debt is issued or guaranteed by substantially the same entities.

- Financial policy moved from deleveraging towards returns: the dividend was reinstated at USD 0.15 per share in December 2025 and a USD 2.5 billion repurchase program was approved in March 2026, alongside debt repayment of USD 2,186 million in nine months 2026 and the redemption of the 7.00% notes due 2029.

Basis: 10-K_2025-11-30_ccl-20251130.htm.jsonl, page 62; EX-99.1_2026-03-27_a20261qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 10; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 3

- Security and guarantees were released alongside the rating upgrades: the 7.88% 2027 and 4.00% 2028 notes ceased to be secured, certain notes and export credit facilities lost subsidiary guarantees, and the company says it has no secured debt after the S&P upgrade, so every creditor now sits in unsecured debt whose legal ranking and release terms are in documents that were not supplied.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 10; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 3

- The business depends on advance bookings and carries a funding float: customer deposits were USD 7,639 million at 2026-08-31, new-ship commitments total USD 18.3 billion over the years to 2030 and beyond, and a 10% change in fuel cost per metric ton moves fourth-quarter adjusted net income by USD 59 million.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 5; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 13; calculation B2
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a benign view is that capital returns are rising while the company's own net debt to adjusted EBITDA was 3.1x at the second quarter of 2026 against its target of 2.75x, new-ship commitments of USD 18.3 billion remain, and security and guarantees have been released without the governing documents being available. A debt-funded distribution, a reversal of the release of security, a rating downgrade, or a booking slowdown that shrinks customer deposits would move the view toward higher governance and financial-policy risk; continued repayment alongside returns, with leverage reaching the target, would move it toward lower risk.

Basis: EX-99.1_2026-03-27_a20261qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 3; EX-99.1_2026-06-23_a20262qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 9
### Limitations

- Ownership percentages, board composition and compensation are incorporated by reference to a proxy statement that was not supplied, so the finding that no sponsor or controlling holder is identified rests on the documents' silence and could change if one holds a large stake.

- The indentures, the revolving credit agreement and the export credit agreements were not supplied, so how far debt, liens, restricted payments and releases of guarantees are permitted, and why security was released, are not established; this limits the financial-policy conclusion to observed behaviour.

- The guarantee structure after the unification is described only in general terms and the relationship of Carnival UK Ltd. to Carnival plc is not stated, so which entities stand behind the existing debt is not established.
- No document is dated after 2026-09-29, so events in the 37 days to the as-of date, including whether the planned shelf registration was filed, are not covered.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

The main structural transaction was the unification of the dual listed company under Carnival Corporation Ltd. and the move of its legal incorporation from Panama to Bermuda, completed in May 2026; plc shareholders received Carnival Corporation Ltd. shares one for one and the company reports no material change to its business. A termination agreement between Carnival Corporation and Carnival plc is dated 2026-05-06.

The balance sheet was reshaped by a refinancing program that the 2025 annual report says was completed in December 2025: in 2025 the company issued six senior unsecured note series and borrowed under three unsecured term loans, and used the proceeds with cash on hand to prepay debt of USD 11.6 billion. In December 2025 it settled the 2027 convertible notes with 69.1 million shares and USD 500 million in cash, and in the third quarter of 2026 it redeemed USD 500 million of 7.00% notes due 2029 with cash on hand. No new debt was issued in nine months 2026; the cash flow statement prints a dash for issuance proceeds.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Carnival's creditors are well covered through 2027 by USD 5,720 million of liquidity and record bookings, but net leverage fell to 3.10x only because debt was repaid, as EBITDA rose just 0.52% in 2026, and higher targeted shareholder returns would slow further progress.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation U3; calculation U7; calculation X8; calculation X14; calculation X15; calculation X16

Fuel is the main earnings risk: its price per metric ton was 36.08% higher in Q3 and adjusted EBITDA was unchanged from the prior-year quarter on record revenue, while the company manages fuel through consumption rather than hedges. The next test is USD 12,994 million of principal due from 2027 to 2030, 52.91% of the total. Net debt and leverage after repurchases since 2026-08-31 are not established.

Basis: EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 14; 10-Q_2026-08-31_ccl-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 10; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation X6; calculation X17; calculation X29
### Key findings

- Demand and pricing power are the core support, and they held through a Middle East conflict and a fuel price spike. Nine-month revenue rose 4.79% on capacity up 1.38% and unchanged occupancy of 106.5%, so growth came from price, mix and currency rather than volume, with net yields in constant currency up 2.4% in Q3 and customer deposits and 2027 bookings at record levels. Price-led growth lifts revenue per berth day without more ships, which supports cash flow visibility into 2027, although record pricing leaves less room for further gains.

Basis: EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 1; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 2; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 10; EX-99.1_2026-09-29_a20263qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 11; EX-99.1_2026-06-23_a20262qearningsrelease8-k.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation X1; calculation X26; calculation X28

- Margins, not revenue, are the weak point. Operating income fell USD 70 million (1.87%) in nine months on higher revenue, and the statement-based EBITDA margin eased from 28.64% to 27.51%, while fuel cost USD 223 million more and now takes 12.56% of operating costs. ### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against caution is that demand, pricing and guidance have held through a real stress in 2026: full-year net yield guidance was cut from 2.75% in March to 1.75% in June by 1.00 percentage points and then raised to 2.3% in September, recovering 0.55 percentage points, while fuel rose 36.08% per metric ton in Q3 and the booked position for 2027 is at record levels. Accrual interest cover on statement-based EBITDA rose from 3.49x in fiscal 2024 to 5.39x in fiscal 2025 and 6.79x in nine months 2026, and the guided interest cost for fiscal 2026 is USD 218 million (16.80%) lower than in fiscal 2025. Distributions are also discretionary: the dividend is decided by the board each quarter, the repurchase program has no expiry and USD 1,562 million of it remains, so management holds a lever that does not touch debt repayment.

### Limitations

- Liquidity coverage of principal due to the end of 2027 assumes the revolving facility can be drawn in full, and whether its conditions and the covenants on interest cover, debt to capital and minimum liquidity would allow that in a downturn is not established, so the coverage could be overstated.

- The outlook rests on management guidance and statements about bookings and the 2.75x target, with no independent forecast, peer figures or market prices supplied, so the judgement that earnings will hold and that distributions are affordable cannot be tested against an outside view.

- Cash interest paid is stated only for fiscal years and fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA is not stated, so the improvement in cover is shown on interest expense and statement-based EBITDA; on the company's own definitions the trend could differ.
- The documents end on 2026-09-29, so fourth-quarter fuel prices, bookings and repurchases since that date could move the leverage and distribution conclusions in either direction.

- The rating levels are not stated, so the finding that refinancing access is adequate rests on the company's statement of investment grade at two agencies and on filed coupons, and the cost of new borrowing is not established.
### Strengths and weaknesses

The strengths, in order of weight, are pricing power with booking visibility, scale, cash generation and deleveraging, liquidity and funding access, and a mostly fixed-rate debt structure. Net yields rose through the conflict and fuel spike of 2026 and the 2027 book is at record levels; the company holds 35.65% of global cruise capacity and added 0.92% of capacity in 2025 against 4.27% for the industry, so its own supply is not what pressures price; net leverage fell from 4.28x at fiscal 2024 to 3.10x at 2026-08-31 with free cash flow of USD 3,176 million over the last twelve months; liquidity is USD 5,720 million with USD 10.7 billion of undrawn export credit facilities for ships; and 85% of debt is fixed rate, so a 100 basis point move in variable rates is worth only USD 4 million of adjusted net income in the fourth quarter.

### Business and ownership

Carnival is the largest global cruise company, with 94 ships in eight brands split between North America (64% of capacity) and Europe (36%), and a 35.65% share of global cruise capacity at the end of 2025. Tickets are 65.4% of fiscal 2025 revenue and onboard and other spending 34.6%, and guests from the United States are 55.8% of revenue, so the credit rests on North American and European leisure spending. Guests pay a deposit at booking and the balance before sailing, which gives a funding float of customer deposits of USD 7,639 million against cash of USD 1,220 million (6.26x) and a working capital deficit of USD 9.1 billion that is repaid in sailings rather than cash unless sailings are cancelled. For creditors the effect is cash flow that is visible months ahead and spread across brands, but concentrated in one product, and a float that supports liquidity in a normal booking cycle and becomes a claim in a shock.

### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is price-led, booked months ahead and discretionary. In nine months 2026 revenue rose 4.79%, onboard and other revenue rose 7.41% against 3.43% for tickets, and net yields rose 4.25% in current dollars and 2.46% in constant currency, so currency added about 1.80 percentage points, on capacity up 1.38% and occupancy unchanged; customer deposits reached records. The test of pricing power was the second quarter, when extreme geopolitical volatility hurt Mediterranean bookings and fuel was nearly 30% dearer; management chose to protect price rather than occupancy in the Mediterranean, cut full-year net yield guidance to 1.75% from 2.75%, and by September had raised it to 2.3%. The mechanism is advance booking: the book is at record levels for 2027, so a demand wobble hits a partly sold year, which supports revenue predictability for twelve months, while beyond that it remains cyclical, discretionary and weighted to the United States consumer.

### Cost structure and margin resilience

Costs are largely fixed once capacity is set, so margin depends on yield outrunning cost. In nine months 2026 cruise and tour operating expenses rose 6.27% and selling and administrative expense 7.33% against revenue growth of 4.79%, so operating income fell USD 70 million and the operating margin eased from 18.47% to 17.30%. The company attributes the rise in operating expenses to fuel prices (USD 212 million), capacity (USD 170 million), currency (USD 160 million), the absence of ship-sale gains in 2025 (USD 103 million) and emission allowance costs (USD 54 million), partly offset by lower fuel use per berth day (USD 66 million). Fuel is unhedged, takes 12.56% of operating costs against 11.50% a year earlier, and cost per berth day excluding fuel rose 1.8% in Q3 in constant currency against net yields of 2.4%. Margins can be defended against volume pressure by the cost programme and by slowing capacity, but not against a sustained fuel spike without yield gains, so the cost side is average rather than strong.

### Capital intensity and cash conversion

Capital intensity is high, but new ships are largely funded by export credit. Capital expenditure was USD 3,611 million in fiscal 2025 after USD 4,626 million in fiscal 2024, and free cash flow converted 35.84% of statement-based EBITDA in fiscal 2025 and 43.44% over the last twelve months. New-ship commitments total USD 18.3 billion, of which USD 6.6 billion falls in 2027 to 2030 against export credit draws of USD 5.8 billion in those years, so 87.88% is scheduled to be externally funded and the net cash call on the company is about USD 0.8 billion, with timing differences; the cost is gross debt that rises with each delivery and is repaid over many years. Capex flexibility is limited for newbuild payments, which are contracted, and real for the non-newbuild part, which was USD 0.9 billion in Q4, so EBITDA converts into free cash flow available for debt service, although a growing share is now committed to shareholders.

### Competitive forces

Rivalry is moderate and supply-led: Carnival and its three main competitors hold about 80% of industry capacity, and in 2025 the industry added 4.27% of capacity against 0.92% for Carnival, so competitors' new ships rather than Carnival's own are the main supply threat to price. Entry is a low threat because few shipyards can build and refit large ships and the capital needed is large, with USD 18.3 billion of Carnival's own ship commitments alone. Substitutes are land-based vacations, which cap price in a downturn when households trade down. Buyers are individuals and travel agents, and commissions, transportation and other costs are 12.41% of revenue, so distribution is a real cost but no buyer has pricing leverage over the group. Suppliers matter most for shipyards, whose limited capacity can delay deliveries and refits, and for fuel, where the company is a price taker; the effect on credit is margin and delivery timing risk, not a threat to liquidity.

### Macro, regulatory and technology factors

Political and regulatory factors are material: the 2026 Middle East conflict hurt Mediterranean bookings, raised crew travel and logistics costs and coincided with the fuel price spike, and higher emission allowance costs added USD 54 million in nine months, so these factors act on margin and booking timing. Economic factors matter through the US consumer and currency: 43% of debt is in euros, which partly offsets European revenue, and a 1% move in exchange rates is worth USD 7 million of adjusted net income in the fourth quarter. Strengths: pricing power with a record book, scale, deleveraging to 3.10x, USD 5,720 million of liquidity, and mostly fixed-rate debt. ### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the company guides fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA of about USD 7.14 billion, with about USD 1.30 billion in Q4, Q4 net yields up about 1.7% in constant currency on capacity down 0.1%, and a Q4 fuel price of USD 896 per metric ton, 8.47% above Q3. Tailwinds are the record 2027 book, flat capacity growth over the next twelve months, an interest cost about USD 218 million lower in fiscal 2026 as high-coupon debt is repaid, and the first newbuild delivery in April 2027. Headwinds are fuel, the conflict, rising distributions and capex. Over three to five years the company targets return on invested capital above 16%, adjusted earnings per share growth above 50% from 2025, and about USD 14 billion of shareholder distributions to 2029 at more than 40% of cash from operations alongside 2.75x leverage; these targets support earnings growth but compete with debt reduction for cash, and are management language that the documents do not test.

### Downside scenario

The realistic downside is a summer-quarter shock that combines regional conflict or hurricane disruption with a fuel price near the guided USD 896 per metric ton. The first break is close-in bookings: in the second quarter of 2026 the company chose price over occupancy in Mediterranean sailings, and a longer episode would cost either price or occupancy in the quarter that earns about 41.92% of annual adjusted EBITDA. Because costs are largely fixed, the company's own sensitivities show how it transmits: in the June outlook a 1% change in net yields was USD 60 million of adjusted net income in the third quarter and in the September outlook USD 49 million in the fourth, and a 10% fuel move USD 59 million. At constant net debt an EBITDA fall of 8.71% returns net leverage to 3.40x and a fall of 27.48% to 4.28x. Liquidity of USD 5,720 million covers principal due to the end of 2027 2.03x, 85% of debt is fixed rate so interest cost would not spike, and the levers are to stop repurchases (USD 929 million in nine months 2026), defer non-newbuild capex and reduce the dividend. The main exposures are refunds on cancelled sailings from the USD 7,639 million deposit float, the minimum liquidity covenant of USD 1.5 billion, and refinancing the USD 3,961 million due in 2028. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress in a shock of the 2026 type, which yields rose through, but a deeper or longer shock is not tested by the documents, and the first observable signs would be deposits below the prior year and net yields below guidance.

### Overall credit view

Overall, Carnival presents a strong business profile supported by pricing power, scale, a record booking position and USD 5,720 million of liquidity, but credit quality is constrained by unhedged fuel cost, rising shareholder returns before leverage reaches the 2.75x target, a USD 12,994 million maturity wall in 2027 to 2030 and legal terms that were not supplied. Cash flow durability appears adequate: free cash flow of USD 3,176 million over the last twelve months is substantial, but EBITDA is only 0.52% above fiscal 2025 and a growing share of cash is committed to shareholders. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on holding investment grade ratings and on the company keeping leverage trending toward target. The primary downside path is a summer-quarter demand or fuel shock while distributions are rising. Further analysis would require the debt agreements, the rating levels and a fourth-quarter result. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: fuel and demand shock in the summer quarter with rising distributions.
